title: Distributed Computing, Communication Patterns & Network Segmentation

paras: Source handwriting preserved intact. Corrections are explained with architecture, practical scenarios, commands and connections to previous Atlas chapters.
Original: Multiple independent nodes cooperate over a network toward a common goal, overcoming limits of one physical computer.

Explanation: A distributed system is a collection of autonomous computing components coordinating by exchanging messages. Nodes may be physical servers, VMs, containers or devices. Distribution enables horizontal scaling, locality, fault tolerance and organizational separation, but adds latency, partial failure, retries, duplicate delivery, consistency and observability challenges.

Example: An online course platform runs a frontend on one service, an enrollment API on another and a database elsewhere. A request can fail halfway even though all three machines are healthy. An API timeout does not prove the database write failed; retrying blindly can create duplicate enrollments. Use an idempotency key, durable transactions and tracing.
Connection: Earlier Atlas chapters cover VM/container resource isolation; this chapter explains the protocols and architecture that connect those workloads.

blocks.h2: 3 · Request–response: synchronous does not mean local or physically wired
paras: Source claim: Request–response is tightly bound to standard client–server and depends on subnet ID/VLAN rather than broadcast.

Precise model: A requester sends a request and receives a corresponding response. It may be synchronous from the caller's perspective, but asynchronous APIs and nonblocking I/O can implement the same pattern. HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, HTTP/3 and many gRPC methods support request–response. IP routing handles connectivity across subnets; VLANs only define Layer-2 segmentation and do not inherently determine whether request–response works.

Real example: A user in Hyderabad calls an AWS-hosted HTTPS API in Mumbai. The devices are in different networks; there is no shared VLAN or IPv4 broadcast domain. DNS resolves a hostname; the client opens a transport connection and exchanges encrypted application data.
Verify: curl -v https://example.com , ip route get 1.1.1.1 , ss -tn . A VLAN ID is not included in the end-to-end HTTP request.

blocks.h2: 4 · Messaging, brokers and the meaning of asynchronous
paras: Source claim: Message-driven communication needs a centralized broker, a broadcast ID and VLAN ID; subnet ID is for the broker only.

Real example: An IoT sensor on Wi-Fi publishes MQTT to a TLS-enabled broker in the cloud. A dashboard on mobile data subscribes to the topic. Neither device shares a broadcast domain with the broker. MQTT is an application-layer protocol , not a radio technology.

Asynchronous nuance: The producer need not wait for the consumer to finish work, but delivery acknowledgments, ordering, retries and durability vary by system. MQTT QoS 0/1/2 are not universal guarantees of exactly-once business processing. Kafka partitions preserve order within a partition, not across every partition.

blocks.h2: 5 · Peer-to-peer: peers can still use servers
paras: Source claim: P2P means no central servers, exchanges subnet IDs dynamically and uses broadcast/VLAN for discovery; STUN/TURN are required.

Example: A WebRTC video call often uses a signaling server to exchange session metadata, ICE to test candidate paths, STUN to discover address mappings, and TURN when direct peer connectivity fails. It can work across distinct ISPs and VLANs. BitTorrent may use trackers and/or a distributed hash table for peer discovery.
Nuance: UDP hole punching is constrained by NAT and firewall behavior; VLAN ID is a local network label and generally not meaningful across the public Internet.

blocks.h2: 6 · Subnet address, broadcast address and VLAN ID: three different things
paras: Real example: Two hosts in VLAN 20 on the same switch can communicate at L2 when correctly configured; a host in VLAN 30 usually needs L3 routing and policy to reach them. A cloud load balancer can accept HTTPS from the Internet without sharing clients' VLANs or broadcast addresses.
IPv6 distinction: IPv6 does not use broadcast; it uses multicast and other mechanisms for functions such as neighbor discovery.

blocks.h2: 7 · Switches, routers, access points and virtual networks
paras: Correction to the mapping: An L2 switch forwards Ethernet frames primarily by MAC address within VLANs. A router or L3 switch forwards IP packets using routing tables. A wireless AP bridges or routes wireless clients depending on its configuration. A virtual switch forwards frames between VMs/containers and uplinks; overlays such as VXLAN can extend logical segments over routed underlays.

Example: A Linux host runs two VMs on a Linux bridge; both share a VLAN-tagged uplink. A router enforces ACLs between the student VLAN and administration VLAN. Whether the applications use HTTP, MQTT or gRPC is independent of those VLAN assignments.

ip -br addr ip route ip -d link show bridge vlan show bridge fdb show ss -tulpen # Commands depend on privileges and installed tools. Correction: A “Docker network” may use bridge, host, none, overlay, macvlan or other drivers; it does not automatically represent a separate physical network. Container IP behavior depends on the selected network mode.

blocks.h2: 9 · Guided, unguided and virtual media: separate the physical from logical
paras: Source: Fiber and switches were listed as guided, Wi-Fi/cellular as unguided, and Docker/VPC/vSwitch as virtual media.

Real example: A VPC packet between two cloud VMs may traverse virtual NICs, host vSwitches, an overlay tunnel, physical Ethernet switches and optical links. The logical network is distinct from the physical media underneath it.

blocks.h2: 10 · Worked architecture: training platform plus IoT lab
paras: What each layer does: HTTPS request–response submits the enrollment. A database transaction and outbox prevent lost business events. The worker consumes a queued event asynchronously. The sensor uses Wi-Fi for local radio access and MQTT for application messaging. Separate VLANs can isolate student devices from management, while firewall policies control allowed flows. The API, worker and broker may run in containers on VMs without sharing an IP subnet.

Failure analysis: If a worker crashes after sending a message but before acknowledging it, the broker may redeliver. Use idempotent processing and durable state. If the WAN fails, the sensor can buffer readings locally. If a hypervisor host fails, a cluster manager—not the hypervisor alone—may restart VMs elsewhere.

Secure multiplexed transport over UDP with built-in TLS 1.3
HTTP application semantics; REST is an architectural style, not a separate transport protocol

tables.h2: 11 · Correction ledger: original assertion → explanation → evidence
rows: “Request-response uses subnet ID and VLAN ID”
HTTP API requests use routable network endpoints; an HTTPS client on cellular can reach a cloud API without a shared VLAN.
“Message-driven needs broadcast ID and broker subnet”
MQTT or AMQP broker messaging normally uses IP unicast; cloud publishers and subscribers may live on different subnets.
Peers can use signaling/tracker/relay servers; WebRTC often uses STUN/TURN.
They are specific NAT traversal/relay tools; LAN P2P and other overlay designs may not use them.
Broadcast is an IPv4 network delivery mechanism, not an application endpoint identity.
Fiber/copper are media; switches are active devices.
These are virtual networking systems or abstractions that ultimately depend on physical media.
